```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Two methods can use the same distance-weighted landscape predictor and answer
different statistical questions. Before comparing estimates or intervals, identify
the inferential target, the effects included in prediction and the uncertainty
that the calculation carries forward. This guide connects those decisions across
the existing optimization and Bayesian workflows.

Start with `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for spatial inputs and
optimization, or `vignette("bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` for annual
Bayesian scales. The example here reads the same bundled artificial annual data
and stored NUTS fit used in the Bayesian guides. It does not fit a model or run a
sampler.

Native LM, GLM and time-fixed unpenalized Cox predictions use the original
fitted terms to resolve formula shortcuts such as `~ .`. New data columns do
not change that design. Variables removed with `-` are excluded from prediction
inputs and effect panels; active interactions and offsets retain their inputs.
Original transformation metadata, factor coding, coefficient covariance and
parameter counts are retained. The installed unmarked provider rejects dot
formulas during fitting, so use explicit component formulas for those models.

For ordinary `occu()` and `pcount()` fits, `plot_marginal_effects(type = "det")`
shows the native conditional detection probability using original observation
covariates. For `occu()`, detection conditions on occupancy; for `pcount()`, it is
the per-individual survey detection probability. `type = "state"` shows the state component; `"lambda"` is a plotting
alias for that component in these ordinary classes. ZIP state curves retain
overall expected abundance. These curves set random effects to zero and retain
native confidence limits conditional on the selected spatial scales. Their
response scale is retained for both `link` settings. Keep the original fixed
covariates and transformation metadata; unused random-only inputs are not needed
for a zero-effect curve. Conditional predictions retain their original guards.

## Separate the target from the computation

A likelihood describes the observed responses as a function of model parameters.
A hierarchical marginal likelihood integrates over declared random effects using
their normalized distributions. A posterior also includes population-parameter
priors. A proper prior has total probability one. These targets remain different
even when they share formulas, kernel arithmetic and response distributions.

| Workflow | Target and computation | Interpretation to retain |
|:---------|:-----------------------|:-------------------------|
| `multiScale_optim()` | The selected backend's likelihood, profiling or native model calculation | Preserve that backend's conditioning and covariance restrictions. |
| `multiScale_bayes(method = "sample")` | Posterior with proper population priors, sampled using NUTS | Read sampling and derived-scale diagnostics before interpreting posterior summaries. |
| `multiScale_bayes(method = "laplace")` | Posterior with the same declared priors, approximated jointly by a Gaussian distribution | A finite approximation is not proof of accurate tails or intervals. |
| `multiScale_bayes(method = "marginal")` | Posterior with proper priors, using the supported marginal approximation and optional importance correction | Integration and correction diagnostics belong to this posterior calculation. This is not unpenalized maximum likelihood. |

The word *marginal* describes integration, not removal of priors. An empty
`priors` list selects the documented Bayesian defaults; it does not turn a
Bayesian fit into a likelihood fit. Likewise, Laplace is an approximation
technique, not an inferential target. Do not substitute a posterior objective
for the likelihood required by an AIC calculation. Use the comparison procedures
documented for the fitted backend and its conditioning.

Unpenalized hierarchical marginal-likelihood fitting and boundary-aware SD
intervals remain development work. The public Bayesian method names above do
not expose those private prototypes as likelihood fits or confidence procedures.
See `?multiScale_bayes` for each public method's supported model structures and
diagnostic requirements.

The analytic optimization backends share preparation and prediction machinery
for Gaussian or exponential kernel means and weighted surface SQ. This does not
make their model classes or uncertainty interchangeable:

| Backend | Supported model | Scale and prediction uncertainty |
|:--------|:----------------|:---------------------------------|
| `profile_glm` | Supported Gaussian, Poisson, binomial and NB2 GLMs | Joint covariance requires the existing curvature gates. |
| `joint_nb2` | Boundary-aware NB2 GLMs, including the Poisson limit | Existing boundary and covariance gates apply; one spatial predictor can use `scale_inference()`. |
| `conditional_logit` | Supported one-case choice sets | Prediction SEs condition on scales; joint scale uncertainty is unavailable. |
| `joint_mixed` | Supported Poisson/NB2 random-intercept models | Native prediction SEs condition on scales; joint scale uncertainty is unavailable. |

SQ needs retained raw buffers and explicit row alignment; kernel means need
binned summaries. Estimating other surface metrics' radii uses the refit backend.
Declared fixed-radius metrics enter analytic and Bayesian models as verified
numeric columns, without additional bandwidth parameters. The Bayesian
adapter also accepts weighted SQ, retaining its fixed pooled reference
normalization and proper priors. Optimization's scale-dependent standardization
is not substituted into the Bayesian target. SQ preparation, sampling, Laplace
and marginal approximation retain their existing uncertainty and diagnostic rules.
Connecting SQ to likelihood profiles does not establish coverage for SQ intervals.

The native-refit path also shares spatial point preparation and fixed-row
snapshots across supported model classes. Raster predictions require a retained
preparation descriptor and use conditional coefficient uncertainty. Analytic
GLM/NB2 maps use the same retained information as their point predictions.
See `vignette("feature-compatibility", package = "multiScaleR")` for the
complete feature/method matrix, explicit scenarios, and smoothing contracts.

## Binary responses and comparison with GLM

Numeric `0`/`1` and logical `FALSE`/`TRUE` responses are Bernoulli observations.
`TRUE` represents one success and `FALSE` zero. Use `binomial()` with
its logit link in the initial GLM, or `family = "binomial"` in
`multiScale_bayes()`. A response prediction is the probability of a `1`.
A two-level factor uses its second level as success. For grouped observations,
use `cbind(successes, failures)` with positive trial totals. Logical count columns
retain their zero/one counts and original totals. The original data and fitted
model frame retain their supplied response types. AIC/BIC comparisons treat
logical and numeric binomial outcomes as the same zero/one observations
when retained rows, trial totals and likelihood weights agree. Changed
outcomes or targets still fail the comparison checks.

```{r bernoulli-glm-workflow, eval=FALSE}
# presence contains numeric zeros and ones; habitat matches the preparation.
initial <- glm(presence ~ habitat + temperature, data = observations,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))
fit <- multiScale_optim(initial, inputs, backend = "profile_glm",
  n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

At the same fixed ecological scales, with the same rows, design, offset and
response coding, the analytic binomial response likelihood is the ordinary
binomial GLM likelihood. The profile backend's retained conditional GLM can be
checked against a separate `glm()` fit on those selected predictors. Joint
scale-coefficient intervals additionally depend on the existing curvature gates.
They should not be compared as though they were conditional GLM intervals.
For a covariance comparison, use the same response form and weights. Native
GLM vector and two-column initialization can retain slightly different final
working covariance even when coefficients and likelihood agree. Logical vectors
should be compared with numeric vectors, and logical counts with numeric counts.

The custom engines support a narrower contract than all of `glm()`. The
analytic GLM route supports Gaussian identity, Poisson/NB2 log and binomial
logit links. Its count/binomial weights are positive integer frequency weights;
weighted proportions and arbitrary precision weights are not accepted there.
The Bayesian interface does not accept observation weights. Native refitting
retains the fitted provider's separate family, link and weight conventions.

Integrating over random scale or response effects defines a different
likelihood from a fixed-predictor GLM. A Bayesian posterior also retains its
population priors, even if no random effects are included. Shared Bernoulli
density code does not make these objectives or their intervals interchangeable.
Compare likelihood-based information criteria only for compatible likelihood
targets, observed data and parameter-count conventions. The private unpenalized
integrated-likelihood prototypes retain their development and admission guards.

## Compare N-mixture models on the observations actually used

Mixed `unmarked::pcount` models retain the native marginal likelihood for
abundance and imperfect detection. Count every fitted abundance and detection
coefficient, random-effect SD and mixture parameter. Latent abundances and
realized random intercepts add no parameters; an estimated ecological scale
still adds one. For example, four abundance coefficients, three detection
coefficients and one SD give eight native parameters, or nine with one
estimated Gaussian kernel scale. A fixed-coefficient display can omit the SD
even when native AIC counts it correctly.

Two models can use the same sites and original count matrix but different
visits when detection covariates contain missing values. Model comparison
checks the native used response, including those missing positions and
omitted sites. Inconsistent or unavailable metadata causes an error.

Null abundance models and detection-only models may supply no site
covariates. The native retained-site count still applies. Original response
row names, or original site positions when names are absent, keep site
identities aligned through omissions. Missing site covariates do not bypass
the used-visit comparison.

The `pcount` argument `K` is an integration bound, distinct from the table's
fitted-parameter count. Check that the likelihood is stable to that bound.
AICc and BIC use retained site rows. With repeated groups across rows, this
reporting convention does not validate the small-sample correction or an
effective independent sample size. Read native diagnostics, including
gradient and curvature when available. A finite table or optimizer code
zero does not establish convergence, identifiability or interval calibration.

## Retain the conditional step-selection target

The conditional-logistic backend requires one used step and at least one
available alternative per complete choice set. It preserves an `amt::fit_issf()`
wrapper's original movement proposals and other metadata. Fixed movement terms,
factors, transformations and formula offsets retain their native meaning. A
saved model frame can supply their training values after the original fitting
call has ended, without reconstructing raw inputs from a squared or compound
expression. New-data predictions require those raw inputs and retain learned
training transformations, such as a polynomial basis.

For an existing step table and aligned spatial preparation, the workflow is:

```{r conditional-step-workflow, eval=FALSE}
library(amt)
library(survival)

# Keep these used and available steps fixed throughout optimization.
ssf <- fit_issf(step_data,
  case_ ~ habitat + sl_ + log_sl_ + cos_ta_ +
    offset(log(effort)) + strata(step_id_), model = TRUE)
opt <- multiScale_optim(ssf, step_inputs, backend = "conditional_logit",
  n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

# Correct the original proposals using the selected model's movement terms.
corrected_step_length <- update_sl_distr(opt$opt_mod)
corrected_turn_angle <- update_ta_distr(opt$opt_mod)
```

Movement corrections require terms appropriate to the proposal distributions;
the backend does not add missing movement terms. Conditional coefficient
intervals, including `amt::log_rss(..., ci = "se")`, condition on the selected
kernel scales. They do not include scale uncertainty. Raster relative risks
remain selection scores, while response probabilities normalize over explicit
choice sets. AICc/BIC use native Cox event counts, equal to the number of choice
sets in this supported case. All alternative rows remain part of comparison
checks. This convention does not correct dependence among steps or animals or
establish AICc validity for a particular design. The profile GLM/NB2 and
conditional-logistic backends support native R interactions, crossing and
nesting with numeric kernel predictors. Optimized-predictor transformations
and kernel offsets remain outside these analytic contracts. Joint mixed and
Bayesian formula restrictions remain separate. GAMs use the native-refit
route to retain their smooth and penalty targets. Native log-RSS scenarios
must already contain the fitted standardized kernel values; amt does not
reconstruct spatial covariates or add kernel uncertainty.

## Read the prepared target before fitting

Preparation checks rows, bins, formulas and priors and freezes the reference
design. It supplies no posterior draws or fitted intervals. Here it uses the
existing bundled inputs rather than extracting another landscape:

```{r prepared-target}
annual <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(
  count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site),
  annual$inputs, annual$data,
  scales = list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)), row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2", priors = list(scale_median = 250), method = "prepare"
)
info <- prepared$inference_metadata
info[c("target", "method", "population_priors", "uncertainty")]
```

**How to read the output:** `posterior` and `proper` describe the intended
target and population priors. `prepare` identifies a checked specification,
not a fitted posterior. The uncertainty entries say `not_computed` or
`not_provided`. They do not supply intervals, establish convergence or authorize
prediction from this prepared object.

```{r prepared-assertions, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(info$target, "posterior"), identical(info$method, "prepare"),
  identical(info$population_priors, "proper"),
  identical(info$integration$scale_effects, "not_computed"),
  identical(info$uncertainty$population_parameters, "not_computed"),
  identical(info$uncertainty$intervals, "not_provided"),
  identical(info$metadata_establishes_eligibility, FALSE))
```

## Choose the prediction quantity

Use the stored fitted object, rather than `prepared`, to inspect predictions.
The rows below represent another survey at known sites and years. Future
responses are removed because they are not prediction inputs.

```{r expected-response}
fit <- annual$fits$pooled
surveys <- annual$data[1:3, ]
surveys$count <- NULL
expected <- predict(fit, surveys, kernel_inputs = annual$inputs,
  row_id = "site_year", draws = 400)
knitr::kable(expected[c("point_id", "median", "lower", "upper")], digits = 2)
contract <- attr(expected, "prediction_contract")
contract[c("inference_target", "quantity", "diagnostics_status", "uncertainty")]
```

**How to read the output:** Each row summarizes an expected count under the
included site and year effects. The lower and upper columns are central
posterior quantiles for that expected response. They exclude observation
sampling variation. The contract records joint posterior parameter treatment,
omitted observation noise and the original fit's recorded diagnostic status.
Those fields describe this calculation; the stored example is not evidence of
calibration for a different dataset.

```{r prediction-assertions, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(contract$inference_target, "posterior"),
  identical(contract$quantity, "expected_response"),
  identical(contract$uncertainty$observation_noise, FALSE),
  identical(contract$metadata_establishes_eligibility, FALSE),
  identical(contract$uncertainty$calibration, "not_established"))
```

| Question | Bayesian function | Observation sampling variation |
|:---------|:------------------|:-------------------------------|
| What is the kernel scale for these covariates or groups? | `predict_scales()` | Excluded |
| What is the expected response? | `predict()` | Excluded |
| What observations might be recorded? | `simulate()` | Included |

For a binomial model, a response prediction is a success probability. For
Poisson and negative-binomial models, it is an expected count. A Gaussian
response prediction is a mean on the response scale. A median expected count
need not be the median of future observed counts. See
`vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for worked new-group
predictions and observation replicates.

## Keep group policies and uncertainty explicit

Known groups use their retained joint posterior effects when included. An
unseen group's sampled effect represents additional group variation; setting
that effect to zero gives a reference calculation. Zeroing an effect does not
integrate over its distribution. Within a prediction call, rows sharing an
unseen group share one sampled effect in each joint vector. Keep those rows
together when you need that dependence. Separate calls do not automatically
reuse the same new-group effects.

The response and scale formulas govern different quantities. A response year
effect changes baseline response. A scale year effect changes how the landscape
is weighted. Preserve their separate prediction policies, as well as offsets,
trials, factor levels and row/site keys. A fixed factor coefficient cannot be
invented for an unseen level.

Uncertainty from optimization and native prediction has its own contract:

| Prediction route | Uncertainty to check |
|:-----------------|:---------------------|
| Supported analytic GLM predictions | Requested joint coefficient/kernel uncertainty requires an available covariance and the original eligibility checks. Conditional uncertainty holds the selected kernel parameters fixed. |
| Conditional-logistic predictions | Preserve supplied choice sets and request supported conditional standard errors. Kernel-parameter uncertainty is not added. |
| Native mixed or unmarked predictions | Native standard errors and intervals condition on selected spatial scales and retain the native component's meaning and controls. |
| Bayesian predictions | Retained joint vectors propagate their represented parameter uncertainty and the requested group policy. Observation noise belongs to replicates, not expected-response intervals. |

For native mixed predictions, `re.form = NA` sets random effects to zero; it
does not average over them. For unmarked models, retain the selected native
state, detection or transition component. In dynamic occupancy, initial
occupancy and colonization/extinction predictions are distinct from smoothed
or projected occupancy trajectories.

`prepare_prediction()` binds fixed rows, scales, standardization, choice sets
and native controls in a reusable snapshot. Reusing it does not add uncertainty,
update the fit or predict new locations. Prepare a new snapshot when those
inputs or controls change. Bayesian summary tables and simulations store their
contract in an attribute; prepared snapshots store a named `prediction_contract`
list. Raw posterior matrices and native numerical outputs retain their usual
structure. See `?prediction_contract` and `?prepare_prediction`.

## Check units, support and numerical precision

| Quantity | Meaning and units |
|:---------|:------------------|
| Kernel scale | Distance in the prepared map units. Log-scale model values are back-transformed with the model's retained distance scaling. |
| Scale-group SD | Spread of group deviations in log kernel scale. It is not a buffer radius. For illustration, 0.3 log units corresponds to a one-SD multiplicative factor of about `exp(0.3)`, or 1.35. |
| Response-group SD | Spread of group effects on the response linear-predictor scale. Its interpretation depends on the response link. |

Keep source CRS, linear units and point identities with the analysis. Internal
`unit_conv` scaling is not a conversion between meters and feet. Compact binned
inputs cannot recover historical raster-value or distance-unit lineage. A buffer
inside the raster extent can still contain missing cells. Neither geometric
extent checks nor a large posterior scale reconstructs landscape data beyond
the neighborhood actually extracted. Review support before interpreting scales
near or beyond `max_D`.

Finally, distinguish numerical diagnostics from precision for your reported
quantity. Sampling diagnostics concern the original chains; importance
diagnostics concern the weighted approximation. `diagnose_bayes_scales()` and
`diagnose_bayes_probabilities()` address derived scales and requested fitted-scale
probabilities. Monte Carlo standard error measures numerical uncertainty from
finite sampling, not ecological uncertainty in a posterior interval. A precise
probability does not by itself establish precise interval endpoints or general
coverage. Compact or permuted draws do not reconstruct the original chains.
Unavailable precision, constant events and failed diagnostics remain explicit.
See `vignette("bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

Descriptive metadata never upgrades a rejected fit. A structural check of stored
parameter dimensions does not prove a valid transformation or recover missing
joint dependence. Read the original diagnostics and the conditioning before
interpreting any estimate, map or interval.

## Quick reference

| Check | Where to look |
|:------|:--------------|
| Target, method, priors and integration | Bayesian `inference_metadata` and the fitted backend's help |
| Expected response versus observation replicate | Prediction function and `prediction_contract$quantity` |
| Included effects and omitted uncertainty | `prediction_contract$effects` and `$uncertainty` |
| Fit status and functional precision | Original diagnostics, then the diagnostic function for the quantity reported |
| Fixed snapshot rows and native controls | `?prepare_prediction` |

Continue with `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for optimization,
`vignette("bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` for annual Bayesian models,
and `vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for prediction.

## Validate estimated scales on held-out observations

`cross_validate()` refits scales and GLM coefficients within explicitly defined
training folds. It supports Gaussian identity, Poisson/NB2 log and binomial
logit models through the existing analytic or native-refit machinery. Gamma
log-link and fixed-theta NB2 use native `refit`; estimated NB2 also supports
`joint_nb2`. Existing kernel/metric admission remains in force. It accepts explicit fold assignments, including the whole-site and
spatial splits generated by the helpers below. Mixed, unmarked and Bayesian
scoring require separate qualification. Conditional-choice CV is described below.

Keep related sampling units together when building folds. For example, put all
observations from one site in the same assessment fold when evaluating new-site
prediction. The function checks row-ID membership, uniqueness and train/test
separation; it cannot infer ecological independence from the IDs you supply.

```{r explicit-fold-cv, eval=FALSE}
# Keep raw cell values so that each training fold can learn its own bins.
inputs <- kernel_prep(sites, habitat, max_D = 800,
                      store_cell_data = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
ids <- rownames(observations)
folds <- lapply(1:3, function(k) list(
  analysis = ids[fold_id != k], assessment = ids[fold_id == k]))
names(folds) <- paste0("fold", 1:3)

validation <- cross_validate(count ~ habitat + group + offset(log(effort)),
  observations, inputs, folds, family = "poisson")
validation$complete           # FALSE means at least one planned fold failed.
validation$summary            # Lower held-out scores indicate better prediction.
validation$fold_results       # Check the status of every split.
validation$errors            # Failed folds remain visible and are not retried.
```

Use data row names that match the prepared site IDs. Each split names its
training (`analysis`) and held-out (`assessment`) rows. Rows may be excluded for
buffers or assessed repeatedly; `assessment_counts` records that multiplicity.
Full-data spatial columns are replaced inside the fold. Training buffers alone
determine initial normalization and representative distance bins. Assessment
buffers use the frozen training bins, and predictions use the fitted training
transformations. Keep buffer extents and initial controls independent of the
assessment outcomes. Lean-only inputs cannot reconstruct these training bins
and are rejected explicitly.

Read `complete` before ranking candidates. When any fold fails, pooled scores
remain `NA`; successful partial scores, failed assessment rows, diagnostics and
warnings stay available. Compare candidates using the same assessment targets,
folds and weighting. RMSE pools squared errors before taking their square root.
Poisson negative log scores include count constants. For grouped binomial data,
use `cbind(successes, failures)` and keep frequency weights separate. Binomial
negative log scores average over observation rows, whereas Brier scores average
squared probability errors across trials. Zero-weight or zero-trial observations
remain recorded and contribute no score. A zero probability for an observed
outcome produces an infinite log score, rather than an artificial finite value.

NB2 theta and Gamma density dispersion are learned from training rows only and
frozen for assessment. Estimated Gamma follows native AIC's deviance divided by
sum-frequency convention, separately from the Pearson scale used for native
coefficient SEs. A known dispersion is supplied to a scoped normalized family
before fitting. Estimated nuisance parameters enter native K once; fixed ones
add zero. Native positive-weight row counts, ecological K and coefficient SEs
are preserved. NB2/Poisson count-density comparisons require identical count
targets; continuous and discrete densities cannot be mixed. Per-fold winners
retain actual family/nuisance settings. See the NB/Gamma worked examples in
`vignette("cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

These are plug-in predictions and scores. They add no parameter integration,
future-observation intervals or calibration claim, and they do not replace
native diagnostic checks. Existing priors, uncertainty distinctions and guarded
inference routes are unchanged. Choosing a model, kernel or metric using CV also
requires outer validation or an independent test set to assess the selected
procedure. CV estimates complement AIC/AICc/BIC; they are not Akaike weights.

By default, results keep predictions, scores, fitted scales and compact
diagnostics. Use `keep_fits = TRUE` only when you need full fold models in memory.
Folds run sequentially with one fit worker, and no full-data fitted model is
used as a warm start. See `?cross_validate` for all score and result fields.


### Grouped/spatial folds and model selection

Use `grouped_cv_folds()` to keep dependent sampling groups intact, or
`spatial_cv_folds()` for projected grid blocks with optional whole-unit training
buffers. Both return the explicit ID splits accepted by `cross_validate()`.
Grouped raster preparation is a separate input contract: modern raw-cell
inputs retain validated per-row map labels in each split. These fixed covariate
maps add no random effects or parameters by themselves. Group generation does
not qualify additional model classes for CV scoring.

Ordinary reference GLMs use `cross_validate_glm()`. `cv_tab()` compares only
complete results with matching targets, splits, observed responses, trials and
weights. Per-fold assessment ranks describe predictions; they must not select
that fold's model. `select_cv()` uses native training records or retained fits and native AIC,
AICc or BIC penalties, then scores the chosen model's held-out predictions.
Neither helper adds parameter/selection integration, observation intervals or
calibration claims. See `vignette("cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

For memory-efficient training selection, request `keep_selection = TRUE` in
each CV call. Compact records retain native likelihoods, complete parameter
counts, training identities, controls and diagnostics. Full models remain
optional via `keep_fits = TRUE`. Record-based selection retains the existing
comparability, failure and uncertainty contracts; it does not qualify additional
model classes for CV scoring.

`cross_validate_clogit()` qualifies a separate conditional-choice CV target for
complete one-used-step sets, with native references or supported scalar spatial
backends. Every set stays wholly in training, assessment or exclusions. Scores
average natural-log choice loss over sets while retaining all alternatives.
Native exact/Efron/Breslow methods, event-based nobs and complete K remain in
training selection, including compact choice records. Generic censored Cox,
case weights, robust/penalized terms and other model-class scoring still need
their own qualification. The CV-only null likelihood adapter checks survival's
stored scalar against the complete-set offset likelihood; it does not change
other native Cox objects. Priors, numerical gates, private admission, conditional
SEs and uncertainty distinctions remain unchanged. See
`vignette("cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")` for a worked example.

# Private likelihood prediction components

The private marginal and factorized likelihood prototypes have conditional point
snapshot components. They evaluate an explicit population and realized-effect
state at training or new locations, then reuse the computed link, expected
response and ecological-scale outputs. New locations require the original
prepared training inputs, so their bin values, counts, distances, source
declarations and retained normalization can be checked. Snapshots keep computed
outputs and compact provenance instead of a fitted model or AD tape.

These components do not widen public fitting admission. Fitted adapters require
the original successful numerical diagnostics, selected eligible start and
zero-SD reduction. Integrated effects omitted by a factorized fit require explicit
reconstructed coordinates. An omitted effect cannot silently become zero.
Explicit zero-effect policies describe a reference prediction. The output does
not integrate population-parameter uncertainty, conditional latent variation,
new-group variation or observation noise, and supplies no SE or interval.
Numerical prediction validity does not establish uncertainty calibration.


Supported fixed scaling, polynomial and spline transformations retain training
constants inside nested expressions and transformed offsets. Bayesian response,
scale and coefficient-curve prediction and private likelihood point components
share this preparation. Older retained fits require reconstruction that matches
their original evaluated training expressions. Prediction stops when that check
cannot be completed. Fitting designs, offsets, priors, parameter counts and
uncertainty targets retain their original meaning.

Supported native LM/GLM, GAM, lme4, glmmTMB and time-fixed, unpenalized Cox
predictions also recover a single standard learner inside an evaluated
predictor or formula offset. The retained training column must identify its
original center, spread, polynomial coefficients or spline knots. Missing
attributes or multiple learners sharing one column require precomputed
training predictors or complete saved prediction calls. Point predictions,
fixed-row snapshots and raster chunks share these training definitions.
Their native coefficient SEs still condition on the selected spatial scales.

## A spatial field in the response model

A native glmmTMB response field adds correlated variation to the response's
linear predictor. It does not make the ecological kernel scale vary by location.
Native refitting can retain this covariance while kernel predictors change.
The initial conformance checks cover one shared exponential field, Gaussian or
log-Poisson responses, and selected fixed ecological scales with no year term.
They verify adapter behavior, not recovery, calibrated uncertainty or general
spatial model selection performance. The `joint_mixed` backend retains its
independent-random-intercept guard and does not admit these fields.

```{r native-response-field, eval=FALSE}
# Use projected coordinates in a common physical unit.
dat$field_pos <- glmmTMB::numFactor(dat$x_m, dat$y_m)
dat$field_group <- factor(rep("shared", nrow(dat)))
native <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  y ~ habitat + exp(field_pos + 0 | field_group), data = dat, family = poisson())
fit <- multiScale_optim(native, inputs, backend = "refit")
# newdat must contain its own matching coordinate factors and group labels.
pred <- predict(fit, newdat, new_inputs, allow.new.levels = TRUE,
  se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")
attr(pred, "prediction_contract")$response_spatial_field
```

The contract names the response covariance, coordinate inputs, field replication
and covariance-parameter count. Units are not guessed from factor labels.
glmmTMB's likelihood degrees of freedom count the fitted covariance parameters. The realized field values are not added as separate likelihood parameters.
multiScaleR also counts its fitted ecological kernel parameters. A field's
correlation range and an ecological scale have different interpretations.

Native point predictions and prepared fixed-row snapshots preserve their
mean-prediction SEs, conditional on the selected ecological scales. Setting
`re.form = NA` supplies a zero-deviation reference rather than integrating over
the field. Observation noise and ecological-scale uncertainty remain separate.
For predictions at new field locations, construct new coordinate factors with
the same projected units and prepare matching kernel inputs at those locations.
A raster's constant site scenario does not supply a spatial field at every cell.
For a full-field raster, verify the original fitting coordinates explicitly:

```{r response-field-map, eval=FALSE}
# xy has one projected coordinate pair per retained native fitting row.
geometry <- response_field_geometry(fit, xy, crs = terra::crs(source_raster),
  batch_size = 64, max_memory_mb = 512)
layers <- kernel_scale.raster(source_raster, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE,
  site_values = list(field_pos = as.character(dat$field_pos[1]),
    field_group = "shared"))
map <- predict(fit, layers, se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional",
  native_args = list(allow.new.levels = TRUE),
  raster_args = list(field_geometry = geometry))
terra::plot(map)  # Native expected-response mean and conditional mean SE
```

New positions require the explicit `allow.new.levels = TRUE` control shown
above. The adapter fails clearly before a new-position batch enters native
prediction if that control is missing or false. Other native warnings remain
visible. Each cell supplies its own projected position rather than repeating the selected
position scenario. The shared group must match the original field. Coordinate
order, factor encoding and units are checked against retained native rows. The declared CRS must describe those original coordinates. No coordinates are
silently rescaled or transformed. Only two-dimensional projected horizontal
CRSs are accepted, including when reloading a descriptor. Geocentric,
vertical and compound definitions must be replaced explicitly with the
intended map CRS before fitting. Fit and requested SE bands remain present
when some or all cells have missing predictors. A different CRS, edited fitting context or
changed descriptor fails before prediction. Recreate the descriptor after an
intentional change.

Native calls use serial sub-batches. A conservative dense-array estimate must
fit the declared MiB budget before field expansion. This guards a planned working
set, not an operating-system memory cap or an exact accounting of native tapes.
Smaller batches reduce expansion but repeat preparation. The initial map adapter
qualifies one shared exponential Gaussian or log-Poisson field. Correlated joint
scale fitting, cross-row raster covariance and spatial mixed-model CV remain
separate gates. The checked layout is glmmTMB1.1.14. Gaussian
and Matern covariance layout witnesses are not fitted-model qualification.

Ordinary unmarked `pcount` and `occu` effect curves instead freeze each learner
from the original raw site covariates before site removal. This supports
nested bases without reconstructing raw inputs from evaluated columns.
The curves retain the native state or abundance target and coefficient
uncertainty. Other prediction components keep their existing requirements.


For ordinary unmarked occupancy and `pcount` state/detection predictions,
point rows, prepared outputs and raster chunks use the original raw training
transformations. Supported fixed scaling, polynomial and spline calls retain
those constants inside nested expressions and offsets. Training reconstruction
must match the retained fitted design and offsets. Keep the original covariates
and design; this comparison cannot authenticate edits that leave the evaluated
training design unchanged. Other unmarked classes retain their native requirements.

Factor contrasts, site removal and observation layout follow the native fit.
If native row removal discarded contrast metadata, unambiguous original
columns for factor main effects recover its coding exactly. Other missing coding needs explicit
saved training contrasts.
Frame subsets retain the original known-group columns; zero-effect requests
can omit random-only grouping inputs.
Native component dispatch preserves detection, occupancy and count meanings,
including ZIP abundance. Metadata are checked once per preparation or map call,
and the native predictor retains its bounded covariance chunks. Confidence
limits and SEs condition on the selected ecological scales and add no observation
noise. Any non-NULL unmarked `re.form` sets random effects to zero, rather than
selecting a subset or integrating over their distribution. Conditional learned random-effect
transformations need precomputed original training predictors; zero-effect
requests do not evaluate unused random terms.


Ordinary unmarked occupancy and `pcount` effect curves use the same checked
native target as point and raster predictions. This includes the overall ZIP
abundance mean and its native confidence bounds. Curves set random effects to
zero. This is neither an average over their distribution nor a future-count
interval, and the selected ecological scales remain fixed.

A zero-effect request needs its original fixed design and offsets. It does not
evaluate unused learned random slopes or require new random-only covariates.
Conditional-effect requests retain their original random-design checks. A
prepared zero-effect context cannot subsequently supply conditional effects.
Ordinary native S4 control abbreviations follow exact-first argument matching
before policy and provenance are recorded, including `re.f = NA`.


Ordinary unmarked curve lists carry a `prediction_contract` recording zero
random effects, no random-effect integration and native confidence limits
conditional on the selected ecological scales. This metadata does not establish
fit eligibility or interval calibration.


### Component-specific unmarked prediction preparation

For ordinary occupancy and `pcount` fits, explicit prediction tables prepare
only the requested state or detection component's original training metadata.
Prepared table outputs, raster chunks and effect curves use that same checked
basis. For example, conditional detection predictions can be evaluated without
reconstructing an unrelated learned abundance random slope. The requested
component still needs every fixed transformation, offset, contrast and, for
conditional predictions, its own original random design. These checks are not
relaxed when another component is unused.

A native `unmarkedFrame` input has a different dependency. Its missing-row
removal uses both regression designs before selecting the prediction component.
Frame inputs and predictions with omitted `newdata` therefore retain both
components' preparation and validation. This preserves native site and survey
row handling. Spatial input preparation retains its existing source and
normalization requirements.

ZIP state predictions remain overall expected abundance. They retain the native
zero-inflation estimate and its contribution to uncertainty, even though they
do not need the detection design for an explicit prediction table. Component
selection does not reduce the fitted model's parameter count, alter its
likelihood or diagnostics, integrate random effects, or include uncertainty in
the selected spatial scales. A component mean or confidence limit still does
not define the joint held-out density needed for N-mixture cross-validation.
